external_prereqs: heat flows from hot to cold

misconceptions.statement: Solids do not change size when heated; only liquids and gases expand.
misconceptions.why: A heated iron rod looks exactly the same, so students think nothing changed.
misconceptions.fix: Solids also expand when heated and contract when cooled, but the change is very small and needs careful measurement to see.

probe.question: A metal rod is heated strongly. Does its length change?
probe.wrong_answer: No, solids are hard and keep the same size.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not change
misconceptions.source_hint: research on children's ideas about thermal expansion of solids

misconceptions.statement: All solids expand by the same amount when heated equally.
misconceptions.why: Students generalise from one example such as iron to every solid.
misconceptions.fix: Different materials expand by different amounts; for example aluminium and brass expand more than iron for the same rise in temperature.

probe.question: Equal brass and iron strips are heated by the same amount. Which one lengthens more?
probe.wrong_answer: Both lengthen equally.

misconceptions.root_belief: similar things behave in exactly the same way

misconceptions.statement: A heated solid expands so much that anyone can see the change.
misconceptions.why: Diagrams exaggerate the expansion so it can be seen on paper.
misconceptions.fix: The expansion of solids is tiny compared with their size, which is why gaps of only a few millimetres are enough for rails.

probe.question: A 10 m steel rail is heated by 40 degrees C. By about how much does it lengthen?
probe.wrong_answer: By about half a metre.

misconceptions.root_belief: real effects are always big enough to see

misconceptions.statement: Solids expand more than liquids because solids are harder and stronger.
misconceptions.why: Students link strength or hardness with greater response to heat.
misconceptions.fix: Liquids expand more than solids because their particles are held together less strongly.

probe.question: Equal volumes of iron and kerosene are heated by the same amount. Which expands more?
probe.wrong_answer: Iron, because it is stronger.

misconceptions.root_belief: hard or strong things respond more strongly

misconceptions.statement: A liquid expands only when it is boiling.
misconceptions.why: Students only notice a change in water when it bubbles or turns to steam.
misconceptions.fix: A liquid expands steadily as its temperature rises, long before it boils.

probe.question: Does the water in a beaker expand when warmed from 20 to 50 degrees C?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it expands only when it boils.

misconceptions.root_belief: change happens only at dramatic moments

misconceptions.statement: The liquid in a thermometer rises because heat pushes it upward.
misconceptions.why: Students think heat is something that physically moves up and pushes things.
misconceptions.fix: The liquid rises because it expands in the bulb and has only the narrow tube to move into.

probe.question: Why does the mercury thread rise when a thermometer is put in warm water?
probe.wrong_answer: Heat travels up the tube and pushes the mercury.

misconceptions.root_belief: heat is a thing that pushes
misconceptions.source_hint: research on students' conceptions of heat as a substance

misconceptions.statement: Gases cannot expand because they already spread out everywhere.
misconceptions.why: Gases have no fixed shape, so students feel they are already as spread out as possible.
misconceptions.fix: Gases expand the most; on heating they spread out to take much more space if allowed.

probe.question: Which expands most for the same rise in temperature: iron, water or air?
probe.wrong_answer: None of them expands as much as iron.

misconceptions.root_belief: something already spread out cannot spread more

misconceptions.statement: A sealed ball swells in the sun because more air enters it.
misconceptions.why: Students link a bigger object with more material in it.
misconceptions.fix: No air enters; the same air inside gets hotter and expands, pushing the walls outward.

probe.question: A sealed football becomes tighter in the hot sun. Why?
probe.wrong_answer: More air gets into the ball from outside.

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger means more stuff has been added

misconceptions.statement: When a solid expands, its particles themselves become bigger.
misconceptions.why: Students assume the whole body swells because every small part swells.
misconceptions.fix: Particles stay the same size; they move slightly farther apart, so the whole body gets bigger.

probe.question: What changes in the particles of a rod when it expands?
probe.wrong_answer: Each particle grows bigger.

misconceptions.root_belief: a whole changes because each part changes size
misconceptions.source_hint: research on students' particle ideas about thermal expansion

misconceptions.statement: Particles in a solid are completely still, even when it is heated.
misconceptions.why: A solid looks motionless, so its particles are imagined as motionless.
misconceptions.fix: Particles in a solid vibrate all the time, and vibrate more strongly as it is heated.

probe.question: Do the particles in a hot iron rod move?
probe.wrong_answer: No, the rod is solid so they stay still.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see is not moving
misconceptions.source_hint: research on children's particle model misconceptions

misconceptions.statement: A metal rod weighs more after it expands.
misconceptions.why: Students think more space taken means more matter.
misconceptions.fix: Expansion changes size only; the mass of the rod stays the same, so it becomes slightly less dense.

probe.question: A metal ball is heated and expands. Is its mass more, less or same?
probe.wrong_answer: More, because it is bigger.

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger means heavier or more
misconceptions.source_hint: research on conservation of mass in thermal change

misconceptions.statement: Rails have gaps only to make joining the pieces easy.
misconceptions.why: Students look for a single practical reason for a visible feature.
misconceptions.fix: The gaps give the rails room to lengthen in hot weather so they do not bend or buckle.

probe.question: Why are small gaps left between rail sections?
probe.wrong_answer: To make laying the track easier.

misconceptions.root_belief: a feature has one simple obvious purpose

misconceptions.statement: Rails need gaps because they expand in cold winter weather.
misconceptions.why: Students mix up the direction of expansion and contraction.
misconceptions.fix: Rails expand in hot weather and contract in cold weather, so the gaps are needed for summer.

probe.question: In which season do rails need the gap most?
probe.wrong_answer: Winter, because cold makes rails expand.

misconceptions.root_belief: any big temperature change has the same effect

misconceptions.statement: A bimetallic strip bends toward the metal that expands more.
misconceptions.why: Students think the longer side pulls the strip toward it.
misconceptions.fix: The strip bends so that the metal that expands more is on the outer, longer side of the curve.

probe.question: Brass expands more than iron. On heating, which metal is on the inside of the curve?
probe.wrong_answer: Brass, as the strip bends toward it.

misconceptions.root_belief: the side that changes more pulls the rest

misconceptions.statement: Hot water opens a tight lid because it softens the metal.
misconceptions.why: Students believe heat makes materials soft or weak.
misconceptions.fix: The metal lid expands more than the glass jar, so the lid becomes looser.

probe.question: Why does a tight metal lid loosen in hot water?
probe.wrong_answer: The heat makes the metal soft.

misconceptions.root_belief: heat softens every material

misconceptions.statement: The lid opens because hot water gets into the thread and makes it slippery.
misconceptions.why: Students think a liquid always acts as a lubricant.
misconceptions.fix: The lid loosens because the metal expands more than the glass; water does not need to enter.

probe.question: A jar is held in hot water with the lid kept above the water. Will the lid still loosen?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because water has not reached the thread.

misconceptions.root_belief: a liquid always works by wetting or lubricating

misconceptions.statement: Water keeps contracting as it cools until it freezes.
misconceptions.why: Most substances shrink steadily on cooling, and students extend this to water.
misconceptions.fix: Water contracts only down to 4 degrees C; below that it starts to expand.

probe.question: What happens to the volume of water cooled from 10 to 0 degrees C?
probe.wrong_answer: It keeps decreasing all the way to 0.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule that works usually works always
misconceptions.source_hint: documented student difficulty with anomalous expansion of water

misconceptions.statement: Water is densest at 0 degrees C, just before freezing.
misconceptions.why: Students think colder always means more tightly packed.
misconceptions.fix: Water is densest at 4 degrees C; at 0 degrees C it is slightly less dense.

probe.question: At which temperature is water most dense: 0, 4 or 10 degrees C?
probe.wrong_answer: 0 degrees C.

misconceptions.root_belief: colder always means denser
misconceptions.source_hint: concept inventory and classroom studies on water density anomaly

misconceptions.statement: Water becomes smaller in volume when it freezes into ice.
misconceptions.why: Students believe solids are always more compactly packed than liquids.
misconceptions.fix: Water expands on freezing; ice takes about one-tenth more space than the same water.

probe.question: A full sealed bottle of water is put in a freezer. What happens?
probe.wrong_answer: The ice shrinks and leaves the bottle part empty.

misconceptions.root_belief: solids are always more tightly packed than liquids
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of children's ideas on freezing and melting

misconceptions.statement: Ice floats because it has air bubbles trapped inside.
misconceptions.why: Students believe things float because they contain air.
misconceptions.fix: Ice floats because its density is less than that of liquid water, as it takes more space for the same mass.

probe.question: Why does a block of clear ice float on water?
probe.wrong_answer: Air trapped inside makes it float.

misconceptions.root_belief: floating means having air inside
misconceptions.source_hint: research on children's ideas about floating and sinking

misconceptions.statement: A pond freezes from the bottom upward because cold water sinks.
misconceptions.why: Students know cold water is heavier and assume this holds down to freezing.
misconceptions.fix: Below 4 degrees C colder water is lighter and rises, so ice forms on the top and the bottom stays near 4 degrees C.

probe.question: In winter, where does a pond start freezing?
probe.wrong_answer: At the bottom, since the coldest water sinks.

misconceptions.root_belief: cold things always sink

misconceptions.statement: Fish survive under frozen ponds because their bodies heat the water.
misconceptions.why: Students give living things the power to control their surroundings.
misconceptions.fix: Fish survive because the ice layer insulates the pond and the water below stays above 0 degrees C, near 4 degrees C.

probe.question: Why does water under the ice of a frozen pond not freeze?
probe.wrong_answer: Fish keep the water warm with their body heat.

misconceptions.root_belief: living things control their surroundings
